column1: # Hmong kinship terms mapped to KinDiv concepts.
# KinDiv <https://github.com/.../KinDiv> is a database of lexical diversity in the
# kinship domain: 198 concepts, mostly Murdock kin types, 1,904 words in 168 languages,
# 37,370 recorded lexical gaps. It has **no Hmong at all**, so this mapping is a
# contribution in both directions -- it gives our kinship terms a cross-lingually
# comparable identifier, and it gives KinDiv a language it lacks.
# Why this matters more than it looks. English does not lexicalise most of the
# distinctions Hmong makes here, so English WordNet has no lemma for them and the
# interlingual index has no concept: 23 of our 37 kinship senses would otherwise
# have to be proposed from scratch. KinDiv already has 19 of those concepts (the
# other four are collective terms such as `kwv tij`), each with a stable
# identifier (`dc:identifier="KinDiv:Fa;El;Br"`) that holds across languages even
# where CILI does not reach, and for 37 of its concepts an ILI as well.
# COLUMNS
#   WH, GM        the Hmong forms, from White (2021) Table 29, p. 288.
#   GLOSS         White's gloss.
#   KINDIV        the Murdock kin-type code, exactly as KinDiv's `concepts` writes
#                 it. `x;` prefixes a male-speaking concept, `o;` female-speaking,
#                 `El;` elder, `Yn;` younger.
#   KINDIV_LABEL  KinDiv's own label for that concept, for readability.
#   RELATION      how the Hmong sense stands to the KinDiv concept, on the same
#                 three-way scheme the Concepticon bridge uses:
#                   exact    the two pick out the same set
#                   broader  the KinDiv concept is broader than the Hmong sense
#                   narrower the KinDiv concept is narrower than the Hmong sense
#                   proposed the concept does not yet exist in KinDiv and we have
#                            proposed it (none at present)
#                 Only `exact` rows should become a link without review.
#   NOTE          why, where the relation is not exact.
#   ORIGIN        where the code comes from: `Murdock` for Murdock's (1970) kin
#                 types as KinDiv records them, `KinDiv` for codes KinDiv
#                 itself added (from Wiktionary), and `extension` for the
#                 nuclear-family codes (Fa, Mo, So, Da, Hu, Wi, So;Wi, Da;Hu)
#                 that are only in our extension of KinDiv
#                 (github.com/fcbond/KinDiv, wn/extra-concepts.tsv), not in
#                 the published release.
# The four cousin rows were once `proposed`, on the reading that Hmong `nus`, `muam`,
# `tij laug` and `kwv` cover the child of a father's sibling of either sex. Nathan
# White (October 2026) confirms they do not: like the clan, they extend only to the
# father's BROTHER's children (cf. White 2021: 287, "Members of the same clan and
# generation are considered 'brothers'"). So they map to KinDiv's existing
# `Fa;Br;*` concepts -- `nus` and `muam` exactly, `tij laug` and `kwv` to the
# age-marked concepts, which are broader because KinDiv does not mark the speaker's
# sex -- and nothing needs proposing. Cousins through the father's sister use other
# terms: not `npawg` or `muam npaws` either, so their `Mo;Sb;*` mappings stand
# (Nathan White, 2026-10-17). He is checking the literature for those terms; Table 29
# (White 2021: 288) does not list them.
# KinDiv's `wn/extra-concepts.tsv` has since added parents, children, spouses and
# in-laws, which brought eight more Hmong terms into scope: `niam` 'mother', `txiv`
# 'father' and 'husband', `tub` 'son', `ntxhais` 'daughter', `poj niam` 'wife',
# `nyab` 'daughter-in-law', `vauv` 'son-in-law'.
# Still unmapped, and still needing a concept from somewhere: `yawg koob` 'ancestor',
# and the coordinate compounds `kwv tij` 'brothers, patrilineal relatives' and `neej
# tsa` 'in-laws, matrilineal relatives'. Those last two are the genuinely novel
# concepts in the set -- a set of relatives defined by descent line rather than by a
# path from ego -- and no kinship resource we have looked at has them.
